about: Storylines for the Stories page (stories.html), written by hand and checked by the site build (work/stories_parts.py). A storyline puts the printed pieces of one affair in the order the papers printed them. Each piece is a reviewed group of the storyline's year; 'quote' is the printing whose opening is shown beside its scan, and it must be located on its scan with a faithful transcription. 'set' notes say how one paper set the piece (headings, lead-ins, changed words), from that printing's scan verdict. Act paragraphs use only what the papers printed. Every phrase in single curly quotes is checked against the printed text, the group's definition or the scan verdicts; {K.first}, {K.last}, {K.papers}, {K.more}, {K.weeks}, {K.firstpaper}, {K.firstwd} and {K.signed} are filled from the data for piece K.

storylines.title: ‘Not to be intimidated by menace’: the Chesapeake affair
storylines.standfirst: A British warship fires on an American frigate off the Virginia capes. Over six months the papers print the account, the President's answer, a British commodore's threat and a town's reply, the order behind the attack, and the verdicts of November.

mark.label: 22 June, the attack
mark.title: 22 June 1807: the attack, as the papers printed it

voices.ship: The commodore · on board the Bellona, Hampton Roads

pieces.says: The Leopard, one of the British squadron at the capes, followed the Chesapeake out to sea, demanded three men said to be deserters, and fired on her until she struck.
set: heads it ‘BRITISH OUTRAGE.’ under its dateline, ‘Friday, June 26’: the earliest printing found
‘BRITISH OUTRAGE!’; its paragraph stops at ‘by our fellow citizens.’, without the sentences ‘feelings which cannot … naval annals’
sets a heading of its own above the account: ‘MORE THAN A “SPECK OF WAR.”’
‘We give the public, (says Mr. Jefferson's official paper) the particulars …’
prints ‘On Monday, June 22,’ where Washington had ‘On Monday last’

pieces.says: All armed vessels bearing commissions under the British government are to leave the harbours and waters of the United States, and all intercourse with them is forbidden.
set: printed it first in an extra the night before, as the paper says, and again in its regular issue
prints the dateline ‘Washington-City, July 2, 1807.’ between the heading and the text
heads it ‘PRESIDENT OF THE U. STAES OF AMERICA’, a printer's slip

pieces.who: Commodore Douglas, on board the Bellona
pieces.says: Unless the committee's resolution against any communication with the British consul and ships is annulled, he will stop every vessel bound in or out of Norfolk; it rests with the inhabitants ‘either to engage in a war or remain on terms of peace’.
set: prints the letter under the Norfolk Ledger's own heading, ‘WAR INEVITABLE!!!’
prints ‘his ships in Lynnhaven Bay’, without the words ‘lying at anchor’

pieces.who: Richard E. Lee, Mayor of Norfolk
pieces.says: The ban was an act of individuals, not of the government; the inhabitants will protect themselves against any aggression.
set: ‘your menacing letter of yesterday this moment’, as the Alexandria and Martinsburg papers print it; six papers have no ‘this moment’
‘the false shew of sincerity’, where the others have ‘security’

pieces.who: Littleton W. Tazewell, who carried the answer
pieces.says: On board the Bellona, Douglas said his letter had been misapprehended, and that he intended no menace.
set: names its source: ‘—Ledger.’, the Norfolk Gazette and Publick Ledger
prints a shorter account in the third person, ‘to give an idea of what passed at the interview’

pieces.says: Every circumstance has been discussed with the gentlemen who carried the Mayor's answer; he will use every exertion, consistent with the honour of the British flag, toward an amicable end.
set: sets its own heading: ‘COM. DOUGLAS'S SECOND LETTER.’
puts it under ‘By this Morning's Mail.’

pieces.who: Vice-Admiral George Cranfield Berkeley, at Halifax
pieces.says: If his captains meet the Chesapeake at sea, they are to show her captain this order and search her for the deserters named in its margin.
set: prints the admiral's middle name ‘Granfield’, as far as the scan shows; the others ‘Cranfield’
heads it ‘IMPORTANT ORDER;’ and spells the admiral ‘BERKLEY’
prints it again, in a new setting, after a question whether the court of inquiry would make the order part of its report

pieces.says: ‘Great and weighty matters’ require Congress to meet at Washington on Monday 26 October.
set: keeps it in its columns seven times, as a standing notice
in one of those, signed by the printer's error ‘JAMES MADSISON’
prints ‘from an extraordinary occasion’ (for ‘form’) and leaves out ‘then and there to assemble in Congress’

pieces.says: The message turns to the British answer on the treaty, the attack on the Chesapeake and the proclamation that followed, the defence of the ports, and the Burr trials.
set: prints it in an Enquirer Extra of 30 October
prints ‘which had so long guided’ and ‘the proceedings of their councils’, without ‘public’, as the Portland Gazette does

pieces.who: A naval court of inquiry, on board the Chesapeake
pieces.says: On the conduct of Commodore James Barron: among other findings, that the Chesapeake was prematurely surrendered when she was nearly prepared for battle.
set: prints ‘Court of Inquiry’, where the others have ‘Enquiry’
quotes the court's 25th finding inside an editorial credited to the Democratic Press

pieces.who: Mr. Blount, for a committee of the House
pieces.says: The outrage on the Chesapeake ‘has been stamped with circumstances of indignity and insult’ with scarcely a parallel.
set: prints ‘the state & navy departments’ with an ampersand, where the others have ‘and’

acts.title: The attack
acts.text: On {A.firstwd} the {A.firstpaper} in Washington printed the first account in this archive, under the heading ‘British Outrage’: on the Monday before, the British ship Leopard had followed the American frigate Chesapeake out to sea, demanded three men said to be deserters, and fired on her until she struck. By {A.last}, {A.more} more papers had printed the same account, from Alexandria to Portland, and each set it in its own way.

machine.text: Reading this story found something wrong in the archive itself. The machine transcription of this issue of the Herald of the United States is filed one page off its scans. A check of the whole archive then found 133 issues filed under the wrong page; data release v0.8.1 corrects them.

acts.title: The President answers
acts.text: On {B.signed} the President answered with a proclamation. British armed vessels were to leave American harbours and waters, and all intercourse with them was forbidden. The National Intelligencer printed it in an extra that night; by {B.last} it was in {B.papers} papers.

machine.text: The Enquirer printed ‘U. STAES’; the machine transcription silently corrects it to ‘U. STATES’. It tidies the printers' slips, so it cannot be used to find them.

acts.title: Norfolk and the commodore
acts.text: At Norfolk a committee had resolved on 29 June to forbid any communication between the British consul and the British ships lying in Lynhaven Bay. On {C.signed} the British commodore, Douglas, wrote to the Mayor from his ship: unless the resolution was annulled, he would stop every vessel bound in or out of Norfolk. The Mayor answered the next day, the Fourth of July: ‘The day on which this answer is written, ought of itself to prove to the subjects of your sovereign, that the American people are not to be intimidated by menace.’ The papers printed the exchange together, with the report of the man who carried the answer on board, and the commodore's second letter.

The machine transcription: ‘LUNGER OFFICE. … NECESSARY INFORMATION!!’

acts.title: The order behind the attack
acts.text: The British admiral at Halifax, Berkeley, had signed the order on {G.signed}: if his captains met the Chesapeake at sea, they were to search her for deserters. The {G.firstpaper} printed it on {G.first}, {G.weeks} weeks after it was signed and more than a month after the attack.
doors: See the affair in the sky

acts.title: Congress called early
acts.text: On {H.signed} the President called Congress to meet early, on 26 October, because ‘great and weighty matters’ claimed its consideration. His message to the special session opened: ‘Circumstances, fellow-citizens, which seriously threatened the peace of our country have made it a duty to convene you at an earlier period than usual.’

acts.title: Verdicts
acts.text: In November two verdicts were printed. A naval court of inquiry, held on board the Chesapeake at Norfolk, found among other things that she had been prematurely surrendered. A committee of the House reported that the outrage ‘has been stamped with circumstances of indignity and insult’ with scarcely a parallel.

after.title: What came next
after.text: The act of 22 December 1807 laid an embargo on all ships and vessels in the ports and harbours of the United States; its printings open the reviewed stories of 1808. Across the whole archive, stories that mention an embargo rise in five waves: 1794, 1796, 1798, 1801 and 1808–1810. Two are American embargoes; the three between are European.
